name: Aluminium and bauxite
summary: Bauxite is the ore, alumina the refined oxide, aluminium the metal. The EU smelts a meaningful share of its own aluminium but mines very little bauxite.
uses: Transport and vehicle lightweighting|Construction and facades|Packaging|Power transmission
eu_note: EU primary smelting capacity has contracted sharply under high electricity prices, shifting the balance towards imported metal.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Antimony
summary: A brittle metalloid used mainly as a flame-retardant synergist and in lead alloys. Supply is unusually concentrated and almost entirely outside Europe.
uses: Flame retardants|Lead-acid battery alloys|Glass and ceramics clarifiers|Ammunition
eu_note: China tightened antimony export controls in 2024, making this one of the tightest critical raw material markets.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Arsenic
summary: Recovered as a by-product of copper and lead smelting. Small market, but hard to substitute in compound semiconductors.
uses: Gallium arsenide semiconductors|Lead alloys|Wood preservatives|Bronze and brass
eu_note: Produced in Europe only as a smelter by-product, notably in Sweden.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Baryte
summary: A dense barium sulphate mineral, used overwhelmingly as a weighting agent in oil and gas drilling fluids.
uses: Drilling fluids|Radiation shielding concrete|Paints and fillers|Barium chemicals
eu_note: Germany and Bulgaria retain baryte mining, so EU dependence is lower than for most listed materials.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Beryllium
summary: An exceptionally light and stiff metal. Copper-beryllium alloys account for most consumption.
uses: Copper-beryllium alloys|Aerospace structures|X-ray windows|Nuclear applications
eu_note: No EU extraction or primary processing. Supply depends almost entirely on the United States and China.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Bismuth
summary: A heavy, low-toxicity metal increasingly used to replace lead. Produced almost entirely as a by-product of lead and copper refining.
uses: Lead-free solders and brasses|Pharmaceuticals|Metallurgical additives|Pigments
eu_note: Strategic since 2024. Because it is a by-product, supply cannot easily be increased on demand.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Boron
summary: Borate minerals. Turkey holds the majority of the world's economic reserves, giving it a position matched by few other commodities.
uses: Glass fibre and borosilicate glass|Fertilisers|Permanent magnets (NdFeB)|Detergents and ceramics
eu_note: One of the most concentrated supplies on the entire list: a single country holds roughly three quarters of it.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Cobalt
summary: A battery cathode metal, mined mostly as a by-product of copper in the Democratic Republic of Congo and refined mostly in China.
uses: Li-ion battery cathodes|Superalloys for jet engines|Hard metals and cutting tools|Catalysts
eu_note: Finland hosts the EU's main cobalt refining capacity, one of the few places outside China able to produce battery-grade cobalt chemicals.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Coking coal
summary: Metallurgical coal used to make coke for blast-furnace steelmaking. Distinct from thermal coal burnt for power.
uses: Blast furnace steelmaking|Foundry coke|Carbon electrodes
eu_note: Poland and Czechia are the EU producers. Demand should fall as steelmaking shifts to hydrogen and electric arc routes.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Copper
summary: The backbone conductor of electrification. The concern here is demand growth and permitting rather than geological scarcity.
uses: Electrical wiring and cabling|Grid infrastructure|Motors and generators|Plumbing and roofing
eu_note: Added as a strategic raw material in 2024 on the strength of electrification demand, not supply concentration. Europe retains substantial mining and smelting.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Feldspar
summary: An abundant aluminosilicate used as a flux in glass and ceramics. The EU is itself a major producer.
uses: Ceramics and tiles|Container and flat glass|Fillers|Enamels
eu_note: Italy is among the largest producers in the world, so EU import dependence is comparatively low.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Fluorspar
summary: Calcium fluoride, the entry point for essentially all fluorine chemistry, including refrigerants and battery electrolyte salts.
uses: Hydrofluoric acid and fluorochemicals|Aluminium smelting flux|Steel flux|Battery electrolyte salts
eu_note: Spain, Germany and Bulgaria mine fluorspar, giving the EU a partial domestic base.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Gallium
summary: A by-product of alumina refining, essential to compound semiconductors. Almost all primary supply is Chinese.
uses: Gallium nitride power electronics|LEDs and laser diodes|Radar and 5G amplifiers|Photovoltaics
eu_note: China imposed export licensing on gallium in 2023. EU primary output has ceased; recovery from existing alumina refineries is the obvious way back in.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Germanium
summary: Recovered from zinc refining residues and coal fly ash. Central to infrared optics and fibre-optic networks.
uses: Infrared optics and night vision|Fibre-optic cable|Satellite solar cells|Polymerisation catalysts
eu_note: Also placed under Chinese export licensing in 2023. Belgium, Finland and France recover germanium from zinc residues, which is why EU dependence is lower than for gallium.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Hafnium
summary: A zirconium by-product with an unusual profile: France is the leading world producer, so the EU is a net exporter.
uses: Superalloys for turbine blades|Nuclear control rods|Semiconductor gate dielectrics|Plasma cutting electrodes
eu_note: The rare case on this list where the EU controls supply rather than depending on it.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Helium
summary: Extracted from natural gas, and irreplaceable for cryogenics. Once vented, it is gone.
uses: MRI scanner cooling|Semiconductor manufacturing|Leak detection|Lifting gas
eu_note: Poland's Odolanow plant is the only significant EU source.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Heavy rare earth elements
summary: Dysprosium, terbium, yttrium and the rest of the heavy group. Rarer and harder to separate than the light group.
uses: High-temperature magnet additives (Dy, Tb)|Phosphors|Lasers|Nuclear control rods
eu_note: Heavy rare earth separation is effectively a Chinese monopoly. Even ore mined elsewhere is usually separated in China.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Light rare earth elements
summary: Neodymium, praseodymium, lanthanum and cerium. Neodymium and praseodymium drive permanent magnet demand.
uses: NdFeB permanent magnets|Electric vehicle traction motors|Wind turbine generators|Fluid cracking catalysts
eu_note: Estonia (Narva) and France (La Rochelle) operate the EU's only rare earth separation plants. Sweden's Per Geijer discovery is the largest known EU deposit.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Lithium
summary: The defining battery metal. Australia and Chile dominate extraction; China dominates refining into battery-grade chemicals.
uses: Li-ion battery cathodes and electrolytes|Ceramics and glass|Lubricating greases|Continuous casting fluxes
eu_note: Several EU mines and refineries are in construction or permitting. None is yet at full production, so the refining gap matters more than the mining gap.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Magnesium
summary: Used to alloy and lighten aluminium, and in die casting. Among the most concentrated supplies of any critical raw material.
uses: Aluminium alloying|Die-cast automotive parts|Steel desulphurisation|Titanium production
eu_note: EU primary production ended in 2001. A Chinese supply interruption in 2021 briefly threatened to halt European aluminium alloy output altogether.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Manganese
summary: Indispensable to steelmaking, and increasingly to battery cathodes. Bulk supply is African.
uses: Steel alloying and desulphurisation|Battery cathodes (NMC)|Aluminium alloys|Fertiliser micronutrient
eu_note: Battery-grade high-purity manganese sulphate is the strategic bottleneck, and is almost entirely Chinese.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Natural graphite
summary: The standard anode material in lithium-ion cells. Chinese dominance runs from mining through to spherical graphite processing.
uses: Li-ion battery anodes|Refractories|Foundry and crucibles|Lubricants
eu_note: Sweden holds Europe's most advanced graphite projects, but anode-grade processing is the harder gap to close than mining.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Nickel
summary: Stainless steel is the bulk market; battery-grade Class 1 nickel is the strategic concern. Indonesian output has reshaped the market.
uses: Stainless steel|Li-ion battery cathodes|Superalloys|Electroplating
eu_note: Finland is the EU's principal nickel refiner, and one of the few places in Europe producing battery-grade nickel chemicals.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Niobium
summary: A micro-alloying element that makes high-strength low-alloy steel possible. Almost all of it comes from one country.
uses: High-strength low-alloy steel|Superalloys|Superconducting magnets|Capacitors
eu_note: Roughly nine tenths of world supply comes from a single Brazilian operation, a concentration unmatched elsewhere on this list.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Phosphate rock
summary: The raw material for phosphate fertiliser, and therefore for food production. Morocco holds most known reserves.
uses: Mineral fertilisers|Animal feed supplements|Food-grade phosphates|LFP battery cathodes
eu_note: Finland's Siilinjarvi is the only phosphate rock mine in the EU.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Phosphorus
summary: Elemental white phosphorus, a distinct product from phosphate rock, made by very few producers worldwide.
uses: Flame retardants|Herbicides|Food and industrial phosphates|Battery electrolytes
eu_note: The EU's last white phosphorus plant, at Vlissingen in the Netherlands, closed in 2012.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Platinum group metals
summary: Platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, ruthenium and osmium. South Africa and Russia between them hold most supply.
uses: Autocatalysts|Hydrogen electrolysers and fuel cells|Chemical and refining catalysts|Electronics and glass
eu_note: Recycling is unusually effective here. Belgium's Hoboken plant is among the largest platinum group metal recovery operations in the world.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Scandium
summary: A very small market with outsized effect: scandium-aluminium alloys and solid oxide fuel cells.
uses: Aluminium-scandium alloys|Solid oxide fuel cells|Aerospace components|Metal halide lighting
eu_note: Usually recovered as a by-product of titanium or aluminium processing, which limits how fast supply can respond.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Silicon metal
summary: Metallurgical silicon: feedstock for silicones, aluminium alloys and, after purification, solar and semiconductor wafers.
uses: Silicones|Aluminium alloys|Solar-grade polysilicon|Semiconductor wafers
eu_note: France, Spain and Germany retain furnaces, and Norway is the largest European producer outside the EU. Energy cost is the binding constraint.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Strontium
summary: Celestite is the ore. Spain is the leading world producer, making this the EU's least import-dependent critical raw material.
uses: Ceramic ferrite magnets|Pyrotechnics and flares|Zinc refining|Medical isotopes
eu_note: Spain's Granada basin gives the EU a genuinely leading world position in one critical raw material.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Tantalum
summary: Used in the capacitors that make compact electronics possible. Central African supply carries well-documented conflict-financing risks.
uses: Capacitors for electronics|Superalloys|Chemical process equipment|Surgical implants
eu_note: Spain recovers small quantities of tantalum and niobium from tin tailings at Penouta, the EU's only meaningful source.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Titanium metal
summary: Titanium sponge and metal, distinct from titanium dioxide pigment. The EU has essentially no sponge capacity.
uses: Aerospace airframes and engines|Medical implants|Chemical process plant|Desalination
eu_note: The EU melts, forges and machines titanium but imports all of its sponge, leaving the upstream step entirely external.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Tungsten
summary: The hardest workhorse in cutting tools, with the highest melting point of any metal. Europe retains real capacity here.
uses: Cemented carbide cutting tools|Wear-resistant parts|Alloy steels|Electrodes and filaments
eu_note: Austria, Portugal and Spain mine tungsten, and Austria and Germany process it. One of the better-covered critical raw material chains in Europe.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/

name: Vanadium
summary: A steel strengthener, and the electrolyte in the flow batteries increasingly proposed for long-duration grid storage.
uses: High-strength steel|Vanadium redox flow batteries|Titanium alloys|Chemical catalysts
eu_note: Mostly recovered from steel slag and residues rather than mined directly, which ties supply to steel output.
sources: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)::https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1252/oj|JRC Raw Materials Information System::https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/
